column9: stem
column28: explanation
column29: hint

column9: What does the prefix "macro-" in the word macromolecule tell you about these molecules?
column15: They are made of only one element
column16: They are smaller than a single atom
column17: They are found only in plants
column28: Macro- means large. Macromolecules are huge molecules, often made of thousands of atoms linked together. A common mistake is mixing up macro- (large) with micro- (small).
column29: Think of other words with macro-, like macroscopic: big enough to see.

column9: A cross-country runner eats a big plate of spaghetti the night before a race to build up energy for the next day. Which macromolecule is she mostly eating?
column28: Pasta is made from wheat flour, which is mostly starch, a carbohydrate. Carbohydrates are the body's go-to source of quick energy. A common mistake is picking protein because athletes eat it, but protein is mainly for building and repairing tissue, not the main fuel.
column29: What is pasta made from, and which macromolecule gives quick energy?

column9: A forensic scientist swabs a few skin cells from a soda can to figure out who drank from it. Which macromolecule in those cells holds the genetic information she will analyze?
column28: DNA, a nucleic acid, carries each person's unique genetic code, so it can identify who left the cells behind. A common mistake is picking proteins: proteins are built from DNA's instructions, but they are not the molecule that stores the code.
column29: Which macromolecule group includes DNA?

column9: Which of these foods is made mostly of lipids?
column28: Oils and fats are lipids, and olive oil is almost pure lipid. Egg white is mostly protein, rice is mostly starch (a carbohydrate), and table sugar is a carbohydrate. A common mistake is picking egg white because whole eggs have fat, but the fat is in the yolk.
column29: Which food would leave a greasy spot on a paper towel?

column9: A weightlifter wants a food with lots of protein to help build muscle. Which is the best choice?
column28: Meat like chicken breast is rich in protein, which the body uses to build and repair muscle. An apple and hard candy are mostly carbohydrate (sugar), and cooking oil is lipid. A common mistake is thinking any filling food is high in protein.
column29: Muscle is made of protein. Which food comes from an animal's muscle?

column9: The prefix mono- means one. A carbohydrate made of just one sugar unit is called a ___.
column20: monosaccharide|monosaccharides|a monosaccharide|simple sugar|simple sugars|a simple sugar|monosacharide|monosaccaride
column28: A monosaccharide (simple sugar) is a single sugar unit, like glucose or fructose. Two joined together make a disaccharide, and many make a polysaccharide. A common mistake is writing polysaccharide, which means many sugars.
column29: Glucose and fructose are examples of this kind of carbohydrate.

column9: Walruses have a thick layer of blubber under their skin. Blubber is mostly which macromolecule?
column28: Blubber is fat, and fats are lipids. The fat layer stores energy and insulates the walrus in icy water. A common mistake is picking protein because blubber is part of the body like muscle, but blubber is fat tissue, not muscle.
column29: Blubber is a type of animal fat.

column9: Celery is crunchy and stringy because each of its cells is surrounded by a stiff wall. Which carbohydrate makes up those walls?
column28: Cellulose is a polysaccharide that forms strong fibers in plant cell walls. Glycogen is how animals store sugar, glucose is a single sugar, and lactose is the sugar in milk. A common mistake is choosing glucose, but glucose is the small unit that cellulose is built from, not the wall itself.
column29: The name of this molecule sounds like the word cell.

column9: Your hair and fingernails get their toughness from a molecule called keratin. Keratin is a
column28: Keratin is a structural protein. Giving the body structure (hair, nails, skin, tendons) is one of the main jobs of proteins. A common mistake is picking lipid because hair can look oily, but the oil comes from glands in the skin, not from the hair itself.
column29: Which macromolecule builds body structures like muscle, skin, and hair?

column9: Every nucleotide, the building block of DNA and RNA, has three parts. Which list names them?
column14: A protein, a lipid, and a carbohydrate
column15: A fatty acid, a sugar, and a salt
column16: A phosphate group, a sugar, and a nitrogen base
column17: Two glucose rings and an amino acid
column28: A nucleotide is made of a phosphate group, a 5-carbon sugar, and a nitrogen base (A, T, C, G, or U). A common mistake is thinking a nucleotide is made of other macromolecules; it is a small monomer, not a mix of proteins, lipids, and carbohydrates.
column29: One of the parts gives DNA its letters (A, T, C, G).

column9: All amino acids share the same basic backbone. Which part makes one amino acid different from another?
column14: Whether it was made by a plant or an animal
column16: The amino group, which is different in every amino acid
column17: The central carbon, which is a different element in each one
column28: Every amino acid has the same central carbon, amino group, carboxyl group, and hydrogen. Only the R group (side chain) changes, and that is what makes each of the 20 amino acids different. A common mistake is thinking the amino group changes; it is the same in every amino acid.
column29: Look for the part that is shown as a letter (a variable) in the general amino acid diagram.

column9: Melted butter is a liquid in a hot pan, but it turns solid again as it cools to room temperature. What does this tell you about the fat in butter?
column14: It has turned into a carbohydrate
column28: Fats that are solid at room temperature, like butter, are mostly saturated fat. Unsaturated fats, like vegetable oils, stay liquid. A common mistake is thinking it changed into a different macromolecule when it cooled; it is still a lipid.
column29: Compare a stick of butter (solid) with a bottle of vegetable oil (liquid) on the counter.

column9: Antibodies latch onto viruses and bacteria to help your body fight infections. Antibodies belong to which macromolecule group?
column28: Antibodies are proteins. Defense against germs is one of protein's many jobs, along with enzymes, structure, transport, and movement. A common mistake is choosing nucleic acids because antibodies are related to genes; genes hold the instructions, but the antibody itself is a protein.
column29: Proteins do most of the active work in the body.

column9: A potato stores the energy its leaves made so a new sprout can use it later. In what form is that energy stored in the potato?
column28: Plants store extra glucose as starch, a polysaccharide, in potatoes, seeds, and roots. Cellulose builds plant cell walls, glycogen is the storage form in animals, and keratin is a protein. A common mistake is picking glycogen, which is the animal version of starch.
column29: This is the same substance that makes potato water cloudy and thickens gravy.

column9: After a big meal, your liver and muscles link extra glucose into long, branched chains to save for later. What is this stored carbohydrate called?
column28: Animals, including humans, store glucose as glycogen in the liver and muscles. Starch is the plant storage form, cellulose is in plant cell walls, and sucrose is table sugar. A common mistake is answering starch, but starch is made by plants, not animals.
column29: This storage molecule is the animal version of starch.

column9: A single amino acid is a protein.
column28: False. A single amino acid is a monomer, one building block. A protein is a long chain of many amino acids (often hundreds) folded into a shape. A common mistake is mixing up a building block with the finished molecule, like calling one brick a house.
column29: Is one link the same thing as the whole chain?

column9: Match each food test with what a POSITIVE result looks like.
column14: Benedict's reagent :: Blue turns green, yellow, orange, or brick red
column17: Sudan IV :: An oily layer stains red
column28: Benedict's goes from blue to green, yellow, orange, or brick red. Iodine goes from amber (yellow-brown) to blue-black. Biuret goes from blue to purple. Sudan IV stains lipids red. A common mistake is mixing up Benedict's and Biuret because both start out blue.
column29: Two of these start out blue. One ends up reddish, and one ends up purple.

column9: When you eat a slice of bread, your body breaks its starch down into many molecules of the simple sugar ___, which your cells use for energy.
column28: Starch is a long chain of glucose units, so digesting it releases glucose, the sugar cells use for fuel. A common mistake is writing sucrose (table sugar), which is a disaccharide of glucose and fructose, not the unit starch is made of.
column29: It is the sugar measured by a blood-sugar meter.

column9: A student wants to find out whether a saltine cracker contains starch. Which test should she use?
column28: Iodine tests for starch, a polysaccharide, and turns blue-black when starch is present. Benedict's tests for simple sugars, Biuret for protein, and Sudan IV for lipids. A common mistake is choosing Benedict's because starch is a carbohydrate, but Benedict's only detects simple sugars.
column29: Starch is a polysaccharide. Which test is for polysaccharides?

column9: Every amino acid has an amino group on one end and a ___ group on the other end.
column20: carboxyl|carboxyl group|COOH|-COOH|carboxylic acid|carboxylic acid group|carboxylic|carboxyl acid|acid|acid group|carboxy|carboxyl (COOH)
column28: Every amino acid has an amino group (-NH₂), a carboxyl group (-COOH), a hydrogen, and an R group attached to a central carbon. A common mistake is answering R group; the R group is the side chain that changes, not the group at the other end of the backbone.
column29: This group is the part that makes an amino acid an acid.

column9: Which nitrogen base is found in RNA but NOT in DNA?
column28: RNA uses uracil (U) in place of thymine (T). Adenine, guanine, and cytosine are found in both. A common mistake is picking thymine, which is the base found only in DNA.
column29: DNA's bases are A, T, C, and G. Which base here is not on that list?

column9: Proteins, starch, and DNA are each built by linking many smaller repeating units together. What are those small units called?
column28: Monomers (mono = one) are the small units, and the long chain they build is a polymer (poly = many). A common mistake is mixing up the two words: the polymer is the whole chain, not the pieces.
column29: Mono- means one. Poly- means many.

column9: Match each macromolecule to the smaller units it is built from.
column28: Carbohydrates are built from monosaccharides, proteins from amino acids, nucleic acids from nucleotides, and fats from glycerol and fatty acids. A common mistake is mixing up nucleotides and amino acids; nucleotides build nucleic acids.
column29: Match the names that sound alike first: nucleic acid and nucleotide, saccharide and carbohydrate.

column9: Match each macromolecule group to its main job in living things.
column15: Lipids :: Long-term energy storage and insulation
column16: Proteins :: Build body structures and speed up reactions
column17: Nucleic acids :: Store and pass on genetic information
column28: Carbohydrates are quick energy, lipids store energy long-term and insulate, proteins build structures and act as enzymes, and nucleic acids (DNA and RNA) store genetic information. A common mistake is swapping carbohydrates and lipids: both store energy, but carbohydrates are the fast fuel.
column29: Start with the one you are sure of, like DNA and genetic information.

column9: A typical fat molecule (a triglyceride) has one glycerol backbone. How many fatty acid chains are attached to it?
column28: A triglyceride is one glycerol attached to 3 fatty acid chains, which is where the prefix tri- comes from. A common mistake is answering 1 or 2. A phospholipid has only 2 fatty acid tails, because a phosphate head takes the place of the third.
column29: Picture the fat diagram from class: glycerol is the short backbone on one side. Count the long tails.

column9: Sugars, starches, and dietary fiber all belong to which macromolecule group?
column28: Sugars are monosaccharides and disaccharides, while starch and fiber (cellulose) are polysaccharides. All of them are carbohydrates. A common mistake is thinking fiber is not a carbohydrate because the body cannot digest it.
column29: Saccharide means sugar. Which group is built from sugars?

column9: Amylase is an enzyme in your saliva that starts breaking down starch while you chew. Like most enzymes, amylase is a
column28: Almost all enzymes are proteins. Their folded shape lets them speed up specific reactions. A common mistake is picking carbohydrate because amylase works on starch, but the enzyme is a different molecule from the starch it breaks down.
column29: Enzymes are one of the main jobs of which macromolecule?

column9: Which molecule has the shape of a double helix, like a twisted ladder?
column28: DNA is two strands of nucleotides twisted into a double helix. The sugar-phosphate backbones are the sides of the ladder and the paired bases are the rungs. A common mistake is choosing a long polysaccharide like starch; starch can coil, but it is not a two-stranded ladder.
column29: Which molecule has two strands held together by base pairs?

column9: Bacteria, mushrooms, oak trees, and people are very different. What is true about the macromolecules in their cells?
column14: All of them build their cells from the same four kinds of macromolecules
column15: Bacteria are too simple to have nucleic acids
column17: Only the plants and mushrooms have carbohydrates
column28: All living things use carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids. Even bacteria have DNA, proteins, lipid membranes, and sugars. A common mistake is thinking simple organisms are missing some macromolecules; every cell needs all four.
column29: Every cell has a membrane, genetic material, and enzymes. What does that tell you?

column9: The sugar in a DNA nucleotide is a ring-shaped molecule. How many carbon atoms does this sugar have?
column28: Nucleotides contain a 5-carbon sugar (deoxyribose in DNA, ribose in RNA). A common mistake is answering 6 because glucose, the best-known sugar, has 6 carbons.
column29: It is one fewer carbon than glucose has.

column9: The amino acids in a protein chain are linked together by ___ bonds.
column28: Amino acids are joined by peptide bonds, a type of covalent bond, which is why a protein chain is called a polypeptide. A common mistake is writing hydrogen bonds; hydrogen bonds help the chain fold, but they do not link the amino acids in the chain.
column29: These covalent bonds form only between amino acids, so they have their own special name. Think of what a chain of amino acids is called.

column9: Which food is the richest source of simple sugars (monosaccharides)?
column28: Honey is mostly the simple sugars glucose and fructose. Butter is mostly lipid, and egg white and chicken are mostly protein. A common mistake is thinking all foods that give energy are sugars; butter gives lots of energy, but as fat.
column29: Which food tastes the sweetest?

column9: Which of these foods are rich in carbohydrates? Select all that apply.
column28: Bagels and oatmeal are made from grains full of starch, and apples are full of fruit sugars. Butter and olive oil are lipids, and chicken is mostly protein. A common mistake is skipping the apple; fruit sugars are carbohydrates too.
column29: Look for foods made from grains or plants that taste sweet or starchy.

column9: Put these from smallest to largest.
column28: A carbon atom is one of the atoms inside a nucleotide, and millions of nucleotides link together to make one DNA molecule. A common mistake is putting the nucleotide first; a nucleotide is built from atoms, so atoms are smaller.
column29: Ask: which one is a part of which?

column9: Spider silk is a protein. If you broke a strand of silk down into its smallest building blocks, what would you get?
column28: Every protein, including spider silk, is a chain of amino acids. Glucose builds carbohydrates, nucleotides build nucleic acids, and fatty acids build lipids. A common mistake is picking nucleotides because spiders have DNA, but the silk itself is protein.
column29: What are the monomers of every protein?

column9: The shiny, waxy coating on a cabbage leaf keeps the leaf from drying out. Waxes belong to which macromolecule group?
column28: Waxes are lipids. Because lipids do not mix with water, a wax coating seals water in and keeps rain out. A common mistake is choosing carbohydrates because the wax is on a plant, but plants make all four macromolecules.
column29: Which group of molecules repels water?

column9: Carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids are all built around a backbone of which element?
column28: Carbon can form four bonds, so it makes the chains and rings that all four macromolecules are built on. That is why they are called organic (carbon-based) molecules. A common mistake is choosing nitrogen, which is found only in proteins and nucleic acids.
column29: This element is in every organic molecule and in all living things.

column9: Which of these are jobs of lipids? Select all that apply.
column18: Storing energy for the long term
column28: Lipids form cell membranes (phospholipids), insulate the body, and store energy long-term. Genetic information is the job of nucleic acids, and speeding up reactions and building muscle are jobs of proteins. A common mistake is choosing muscle because people say fat and muscle together.
column29: Three jobs belong to lipids. The others belong to nucleic acids or proteins.

column9: The sugar in each DNA nucleotide is called ___, which gives DNA the "D" in its name.
column28: DNA stands for deoxyribonucleic acid. Its sugar is deoxyribose: ribose missing one oxygen atom. RNA uses ribose. A common mistake is writing ribose, which is the sugar in RNA.
column29: RNA's sugar is ribose. DNA's sugar is almost the same, but it is missing one oxygen atom.

column9: A plain hamburger patty, without the bun, is made mostly of which two macromolecules?
column28: Ground beef is animal muscle (protein) mixed with animal fat (lipid). The carbohydrates in a hamburger come from the bun. A common mistake is including carbohydrate; meat has almost no carbohydrate.
column29: A patty is muscle plus fat.

column9: Put these carbohydrates in order from smallest to largest.
column28: Galactose is a monosaccharide (one sugar), maltose is a disaccharide (two glucose units), and glycogen is a polysaccharide (many glucose units). A common mistake is putting maltose first because all three end in -ose; the name ending alone does not tell size.
column29: Sort them into mono-, di-, and polysaccharides.

column9: When you lift a heavy backpack, your muscles shorten. The fibers inside muscle cells that do the pulling are made mostly of which macromolecule?
column28: Muscle fibers are made of proteins (actin and myosin) that slide past each other to shorten the muscle. Movement is one of protein's jobs. A common mistake is picking carbohydrates because muscles burn sugar for energy; the sugar is the fuel, but the fibers themselves are protein.
column29: Meat is animal muscle. What macromolecule is meat mostly made of?

column9: Which of these molecules is a nucleic acid?
column28: RNA (ribonucleic acid) is a nucleic acid, along with DNA. Starch is a carbohydrate, insulin is a protein, and cholesterol is a lipid. A common mistake is thinking only DNA counts; RNA is a nucleic acid too.
column29: Look for the molecule whose full name ends in nucleic acid.

column9: Which test would show whether a potato chip contains fat?
column28: Sudan IV stains lipids (fats and oils) red. Biuret tests for protein, iodine for starch, and Benedict's for simple sugars. A common mistake is choosing iodine because potatoes have starch; that would test the starch, not the fat.
column29: Fats are lipids. Which test is the lipid test?

column9: You rub a potato chip on a piece of brown paper bag and let the paper dry. When you hold it up to a light, a see-through, greasy spot remains. What does this show?
column28: Lipids soak into paper and make a translucent spot that does not dry up. A spot from water would disappear as it dried. A common mistake is thinking any wet spot means fat, which is why you wait for it to dry.
column29: Water dries up and disappears. What kind of molecule leaves a lasting greasy spot?

column9: A phospholipid has a "head" and two "tails." How does each part act around water?
column14: Neither part is affected by water
column15: Both the head and the tails are attracted to water
column16: The head is attracted to water, and the tails avoid water
column17: The head avoids water, and the tails are attracted to water
column28: The phosphate head is polar, so it is attracted to water (hydrophilic). The two fatty acid tails are nonpolar, so they avoid water (hydrophobic). A common mistake is reversing them; remember the tails are the oily, fat-like part.
column29: The tails are fatty acid chains. Do fats mix with water?

column9: Cholesterol and the hormones testosterone and estrogen all share a structure of four connected carbon rings. Which macromolecule group are they in?
column28: These ring-shaped molecules are steroids, a type of lipid. Like other lipids, they are nonpolar and do not dissolve well in water. A common mistake is picking proteins because some hormones, like insulin, are proteins, but steroid hormones are lipids.
column29: Cholesterol is listed on nutrition labels next to the fats.

column9: With a molecular model kit, a student builds two fatty acid chains. One is straight, and the other has a bend (kink) in it. What causes the bend?
column14: A phosphate group attached to the end of the chain
column15: One or more double bonds between carbon atoms
column16: A nitrogen atom in the middle of the chain
column17: Extra hydrogen atoms crowded onto the chain
column28: A double bond between two carbon atoms bends the chain. Chains with double bonds are unsaturated. Chains with only single bonds hold the most hydrogen (saturated) and stay straight. A common mistake is thinking extra hydrogen causes the bend, but the straight saturated chain is the one with the most hydrogen.
column29: Unsaturated fats have kinks. What do unsaturated fats have that saturated fats lack?

column9: Why is butter (mostly saturated fat) solid at room temperature while corn oil (mostly unsaturated fat) is liquid?
column14: Butter's straight fatty acid chains pack tightly together, while corn oil's kinked chains cannot
column15: Corn oil's chains are perfectly straight, so they slide apart easily
column16: Butter contains more water than corn oil, and the water freezes
column17: Butter's fat is actually a protein, which is always solid
column28: Straight saturated chains stack closely, like pencils in a box, so they stay solid. Kinked unsaturated chains cannot pack tightly, so they stay liquid. A common mistake is thinking unsaturated chains are the straight ones; the double bonds put kinks in them.
column29: Think about which shape stacks more neatly: straight sticks or bent ones.

column9: Chitin forms the hard outer skeleton of crabs and beetles and the cell walls of mushrooms. In the job it does, chitin is most like which other carbohydrate?
column28: Chitin and cellulose are both structural polysaccharides: they build tough walls and coverings. Starch and glycogen store energy, and glucose is fuel. A common mistake is matching by organism (animals, so glycogen) instead of by job.
column29: Is chitin used for storing energy or for building structure?

column9: Two juices are tested with Benedict's reagent the same way. Juice A turns green, and Juice B turns brick red. What can you conclude?
column14: Juice B contains starch instead of sugar
column15: Juice A has more simple sugar than Juice B
column16: Juice B has more simple sugar than Juice A
column17: Both juices have the same amount of simple sugar
column28: Benedict's color shows how much simple sugar is present: green is a little, then yellow and orange, and brick red is the most. A common mistake is thinking any color change means the same amount, or that red means starch; Benedict's does not test for starch.
column29: Benedict's colors go in order from least sugar to most sugar.

column9: A person with a very high fever (above 41 °C) is in danger partly because heat can change the shape of proteins in their cells. Why does a change in shape matter?
column14: Heat turns the proteins into fats
column15: Heat adds extra amino acids, making the proteins too long
column16: A protein's job depends on its shape, so a protein that loses its shape may stop working
column17: Heat makes proteins work faster, which uses up the body's energy
column28: A protein's folded shape lets it do its job, so a protein that unfolds (denatures) can stop working. The amino acids are still there; only the shape changes. A common mistake is thinking heat changes the protein into another macromolecule.
column29: In proteins, shape and function go together.

column9: Hemoglobin is made of four separate polypeptide chains fitted together. Which level of protein structure describes how these chains fit together?
column28: Quaternary structure is how two or more folded chains join to make one working protein. Primary is the amino acid sequence, secondary is helices and sheets, and tertiary is the 3-D folding of one chain. A common mistake is picking tertiary, which describes only a single chain.
column29: Only one level of structure involves more than one chain.

column9: Put these steps in the order they happen as a protein takes its final shape.
column14: The whole chain folds into a 3-D shape
column15: Amino acids are linked in a specific order
column16: Two or more folded chains fit together
column17: Short sections coil into helices or fold into sheets
column28: First the amino acids are linked in order (primary), then short sections coil or fold (secondary), then the whole chain folds into 3-D (tertiary), and finally some proteins join with other chains (quaternary). A common mistake is starting with folding, but there is nothing to fold until the chain is built.
column29: Build the chain first, then fold small parts, then the whole thing.

column9: Benedict's reagent changes color depending on how much simple sugar is present. Put the colors in order from NO sugar to the MOST sugar.
column28: Benedict's stays blue with no simple sugar, then turns green, yellow, orange, and brick red as the amount of sugar goes up. A common mistake is putting green after yellow; green means only a small amount of sugar.
column29: The colors follow part of the rainbow, starting from the blue of the reagent itself.

column9: Each molecule below helps your body in a different way. Match each one to its job.
column14: Hemoglobin :: Carries oxygen in red blood cells
column15: Collagen :: Gives strength to skin, tendons, and bones
column16: Insulin :: Signals cells to take in sugar from the blood
column17: Antibody :: Marks germs so the body can destroy them
column18: Actin and myosin :: Slide past each other to shorten muscles
column28: These are all proteins with different jobs: transport (hemoglobin), structure (collagen), signaling (insulin), defense (antibodies), and movement (actin and myosin). A common mistake is swapping hemoglobin and insulin because both work in the blood.
column29: Hemo- refers to blood. Which job involves something carried in the blood?

column9: Match each molecule to the job it does in a plant, an animal, or a cell.
column14: Phospholipid :: Forms the double layer around every cell
column15: Triglyceride (fat) :: Stores energy in fat tissue
column16: Wax :: Waterproof coating on leaves and fruit
column17: Cholesterol :: Keeps animal cell membranes from getting too stiff or too runny
column28: Phospholipids build membranes, triglycerides store energy, waxes waterproof surfaces, cholesterol steadies animal cell membranes, and DNA stores hereditary instructions. A common mistake is thinking all lipids just store energy; different lipids have very different jobs.
column29: Match the word membrane, energy, and waterproof first.

column9: Which of these are found in BOTH DNA and RNA? Select all that apply.
column28: Both DNA and RNA have phosphate groups and the bases adenine, guanine, and cytosine. Thymine is only in DNA, uracil and ribose are only in RNA (DNA has deoxyribose). A common mistake is choosing ribose, but DNA's sugar is deoxyribose.
column29: Compare the bases (A, T, C, G vs. A, U, C, G) and the sugars of DNA and RNA.

column9: A serving of peanuts has 14 g of fat. Fat provides about 9 Calories per gram. How many Calories in the serving come from fat?
column28: 14 g × 9 Calories/g = 126 Calories. A common mistake is using 4 Calories per gram, which is the value for carbohydrates and proteins, not fats.
column29: Multiply the grams of fat by the Calories in each gram.

column9: A short piece of DNA is 12 base pairs long. How many nucleotides does it contain?
column28: Each base pair is two nucleotides, one on each strand, so 12 × 2 = 24 nucleotides. A common mistake is answering 12 and counting only one strand.
column29: DNA has two strands. How many nucleotides make one base pair?

column9: A clear liquid turns brick red when heated with Benedict's reagent but shows no change with iodine, Biuret, or Sudan IV. Which could it be?
column28: Only the simple-sugar test was positive. Honey is mostly glucose and fructose, which turn Benedict's brick red. Cornstarch would turn iodine blue-black, vegetable oil would stain red with Sudan IV, and egg white would turn Biuret purple. A common mistake is picking cornstarch because it is a carbohydrate, but starch is not a simple sugar.
column29: Which food is mostly simple sugar with almost no starch, protein, or fat?

column9: When testing foods for protein, a student also adds Biuret reagent to a tube of plain water. Why?
column14: Biuret only works after it has been used once
column15: Water is a protein, so it should turn purple
column16: It shows what a negative result looks like, so the food tubes can be compared to it
column17: Water speeds up the Biuret reaction in the other tubes
column28: The water tube is a control (negative control). It shows the color Biuret stays when no protein is present (blue), so a purple food tube clearly stands out. A common mistake is thinking the control is wasted; without it, you cannot be sure what a color change means.
column29: What does a control group do in any experiment?

column9: Cows can live on a diet of grass, but a person eating only grass would starve. What is the main reason?
column14: Humans cannot digest any polysaccharide, including starch
column15: Grass is mostly protein, and humans cannot use plant protein
column16: Most of the energy in grass is locked in cellulose, which humans cannot break down
column17: Grass contains no carbohydrates at all
column28: Grass is full of cellulose. Cows have microbes in their stomachs that break cellulose down, but humans do not, so the glucose in cellulose passes through us as fiber. A common mistake is thinking humans cannot digest any polysaccharide; we digest starch just fine.
column29: Which polysaccharide makes up plant cell walls, and can people digest it?

column9: A few drops of salad oil on top of water stay together in round beads instead of mixing in. Why?
column14: Oil molecules are nonpolar, so water molecules stick to each other instead of to the oil
column15: Oil is denser than water, so it sinks into a tight bead
column16: Oil is a protein, and water changes its shape
column17: Oil molecules are charged ions that push the water away
column28: Lipids are nonpolar. Polar water molecules are attracted to each other, not to the oil, so the oil gets pushed together into beads. A common mistake is the density answer: oil is less dense than water, which is why it floats instead of sinking.
column29: Water is polar. Are lipids polar or nonpolar?

column9: A student adds Benedict's reagent to apple juice at room temperature. After 5 minutes it is still blue, so she concludes the juice has no sugar. What is the problem with her test?
column14: She never heated the tube in a hot water bath, which Benedict's needs
column15: She used the wrong reagent; Benedict's tests for protein
column17: She should have waited a full day for the color to change
column28: Benedict's reagent only changes color when it is heated in a hot water bath. Without heat, even a sugary juice stays blue. A common mistake is thinking every food test works at room temperature; iodine, Biuret, and Sudan IV do, but Benedict's does not.
column29: Think about the extra lab step that only one of the four tests needs.

column9: A molecule found in a cell is made of carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, and phosphorus. Which is it most likely to be?
column15: A nucleic acid such as DNA
column28: Nucleic acids contain C, H, O, N, and P: the phosphorus is in every nucleotide's phosphate group. Starch and fats have only C, H, and O, and proteins have C, H, O, N (and sometimes S) but no phosphorus. A common mistake is choosing protein because of the nitrogen, but proteins do not have the phosphorus.
column29: Which element is missing from proteins but present in every nucleotide?

column9: A corn plant grows in soil with almost no nitrogen. Which two macromolecules would the plant have the hardest time building?
column28: Every amino acid has an amino group with nitrogen, and every nucleotide has a nitrogen base, so proteins and nucleic acids need nitrogen. Carbohydrates and most lipids are only C, H, and O. A common mistake is picking carbohydrates because corn makes so much sugar, but sugar has no nitrogen. This is why farmers add nitrogen fertilizer.
column29: Which macromolecules have nitrogen in their building blocks?

column9: People who are lactose intolerant can't break lactose, the sugar in milk, into glucose and galactose. Based on this, what type of carbohydrate is lactose?
column28: Lactose breaks into two simple sugars (glucose and galactose), so it is a disaccharide: di- means two. A common mistake is choosing polysaccharide just because lactose can be broken down; a polysaccharide breaks into many sugar units, not two.
column29: Count how many simple sugars lactose splits into.

column9: A student tests four foods with Biuret reagent. Which one would most likely stay blue?
column28: Biuret stays blue when there is no protein. Sugar water has only carbohydrate, while egg white, tofu, and milk all contain protein and would turn purple. A common mistake is picking milk because it is a drink, but milk has plenty of protein.
column29: Biuret tests for protein. Which food has none?

column9: Sudan IV is added to three tubes: whole milk, skim milk, and plain water. Which tube should show the most red staining?
column14: All three would look the same
column28: Sudan IV stains lipids red, and whole milk has the most fat. Skim milk has most of its fat removed, and water has none. A common mistake is thinking all milk is the same; the difference between whole and skim milk is the fat.
column29: What is removed from milk to make skim milk?

column9: Which statements correctly compare carbohydrates and lipids? Select all that apply.
column14: Both are made mainly of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen
column15: Both can be used by organisms to store energy
column18: Carbohydrates are usually the faster source of energy
column28: Both are made mainly of C, H, and O, and both store energy (starch and glycogen; fats). Carbohydrates give quicker energy. Lipids do not dissolve in water, lipids are not made of nucleotides, and neither one needs nitrogen. A common mistake is choosing "both dissolve," since sugar dissolves but oil does not.
column29: Check each statement against both groups. It must be true for both (or compare them correctly).

column9: Three of the four macromolecule groups are polymers made of long chains of repeating monomers. Which group is usually NOT a true polymer?
column28: A fat is one glycerol attached to fatty acids, not a long chain of repeating units, so lipids are not true polymers. Polysaccharides, proteins, and nucleic acids are long chains of monomers. A common mistake is thinking fatty acids are monomers that link end to end; they each attach to glycerol instead.
column29: Picture a fat molecule. Is it a long repeating chain or a small backbone with a few tails?

column9: Doctors often suggest cooking with olive oil instead of butter. How is the fat in olive oil different?
column14: Olive oil is mostly unsaturated fat, while butter is mostly saturated fat
column15: Olive oil has no carbon atoms in it
column16: Olive oil is a carbohydrate, so the body burns it faster
column17: Olive oil is mostly protein instead of fat
column28: Olive oil is liquid at room temperature because it is mostly unsaturated fat. Butter is solid because it is mostly saturated fat, which is linked to heart disease when eaten in large amounts. A common mistake is thinking olive oil is not a fat at all; it is still 100% lipid.
column29: Oils are liquid at room temperature and butter is solid. What does that tell you about each fat?

column9: One strand of a DNA molecule has the bases A-T-T-G-C. What is the order of bases on the matching strand?
column28: In DNA, A pairs with T and C pairs with G, so A-T-T-G-C pairs with T-A-A-C-G. A common mistake is using U, but uracil is only in RNA.
column29: Pair each base: A with T, and C with G.

column9: People with type 1 diabetes usually inject insulin instead of swallowing it as a pill. Based on what you know about insulin's structure, why?
column14: Insulin is a protein, so digestion would break it into amino acids before it could work
column15: Pills cannot hold any medicine made by the body
column16: Insulin is a lipid, so it won't dissolve in the stomach
column17: Insulin is a nucleic acid that only works in the bloodstream
column28: Insulin is a protein. The digestive system breaks proteins in food down into amino acids, so swallowed insulin would be destroyed before reaching the blood. A common mistake is thinking insulin is a sugar because it controls blood sugar.
column29: What happens to the protein in a hamburger when you digest it?

column9: In sickle cell disease, just one amino acid out of the 146 in a hemoglobin chain is different. That one change makes red blood cells stiff and curved. Which explanation is best?
column14: Amino acid order has no effect on a protein, so the problem must come from carbohydrates
column15: Changing the amino acid sequence can change how the chain folds, and the new shape changes how the protein works
column16: The one change removes all of the cell's DNA
column17: The new amino acid turns hemoglobin into a lipid
column28: The order of amino acids decides how a protein folds, and its shape decides its function. One different amino acid makes hemoglobin molecules stick together into long fibers that bend the cell. A common mistake is thinking one small change out of 146 can't matter; even one can change the shape.
column29: Follow the chain: sequence, then shape, then job.

column9: A short protein chain has 60 amino acids lined up in a single row. How many peptide bonds hold this chain together?
column28: Each peptide bond connects two neighboring amino acids, so a chain of 60 has 60 − 1 = 59 bonds. A common mistake is answering 60, but the first and last amino acids each have one open end.
column29: Try a small case: 3 beads on a string need how many connections?

column9: A sample of DNA is 30% adenine (A). Using the base-pairing rules, what percent of the bases in the sample are guanine (G)? Enter the number only.
column28: A pairs with T, so T is also 30%. A + T = 60%, leaving 40% for G and C. Since G pairs with C, they are equal: 40 ÷ 2 = 20% guanine. A common mistake is answering 70 (100 − 30) and forgetting about T and C.
column29: Find T first, then split what is left between G and C.

column9: A student mixes two solutions from the lab shelf and tests the mixture. Benedict's turns brick red, iodine stays amber, Biuret stays blue, and Sudan IV makes a red-stained layer. Which two solutions did she mix?
column28: Benedict's positive means simple sugar (glucose), and Sudan IV positive means lipid (oil). Iodine negative rules out starch, and Biuret negative rules out egg white (protein). A common mistake is choosing starch because it is a carbohydrate, but Benedict's detects simple sugars and the iodine test was negative.
column29: Write down what each positive and each negative result tells you, then check every choice.

column9: A granola bar has 190 Calories. It contains 25 g of carbohydrate and 9 g of protein, and the rest of its Calories come from fat. Using 4 Calories per gram for carbohydrate and protein and 9 Calories per gram for fat, how many grams of fat does it contain?
column28: Carbohydrate: 25 × 4 = 100 Calories. Protein: 9 × 4 = 36 Calories. That leaves 190 − 100 − 36 = 54 Calories from fat, and 54 ÷ 9 = 6 g of fat. A common mistake is stopping at 54, which is Calories, not grams.
column29: Find the Calories from carbohydrate and protein first, subtract, then convert the rest to grams.

column9: A student heats a solution of table sugar (sucrose) with Benedict's reagent, and it stays blue. Her partner says, "Then table sugar isn't a carbohydrate." Which response is best?
column14: The test was done wrong, because every carbohydrate turns Benedict's red
column15: Benedict's detects simple sugars; table sugar is a disaccharide, so a negative result doesn't mean it isn't a carbohydrate
column16: Table sugar must be a lipid, since it failed the sugar test
column17: Table sugar is a protein, so it should have been tested with Biuret
column28: Benedict's detects simple sugars (monosaccharides). Sucrose is a disaccharide made of glucose and fructose joined together, so it can test negative and still be a carbohydrate. A common mistake is thinking each test detects a whole macromolecule group; a negative test only means that specific kind of molecule was not found.
column29: What exactly does Benedict's detect, and what kind of sugar is sucrose?

column9: When phospholipids are dropped into water, they arrange themselves into a double layer. Which description of that double layer is correct?
column14: The phospholipids dissolve completely, like salt
column15: Tails face the water on both sides, and the heads hide in the middle
column16: Heads face the water on both sides, and the tails point inward toward each other, away from the water
column17: Heads and tails line up in a random order
column28: The water-loving heads face the water outside and inside the cell, and the water-fearing tails tuck into the middle, away from water. This is the structure of every cell membrane. A common mistake is putting the tails on the outside; that would put the oily part right against the water.
column29: Which part of a phospholipid needs to stay away from water?

column9: Which choice correctly matches a macromolecule with BOTH its building blocks AND one of its main jobs?
column14: Lipid: amino acids; long-term energy storage
column15: Protein: amino acids; speeds up reactions as enzymes
column16: Nucleic acid: nucleotides; main source of quick energy
column28: Proteins are built from amino acids, and many proteins work as enzymes. Each other choice has one correct part and one wrong part: carbohydrates don't store hereditary information, lipids aren't built from amino acids, and nucleic acids aren't quick energy. A common mistake is stopping after the first part looks right.
column29: Check both halves of each choice. One mistake makes the whole choice wrong.

column9: Fish that live in icy Arctic water have cell membranes with many unsaturated fatty acid tails. What is the most likely advantage?
column14: Unsaturated tails contain nitrogen that warms the cell
column15: Unsaturated fats are proteins that act like antifreeze
column16: Unsaturated tails have kinks that keep them from packing tightly, so the membrane stays flexible in the cold
column17: Saturated tails would bend more, so the fish avoid them to keep membranes stiff
column28: Cold makes fats pack tighter and stiffen, like butter in a fridge. Kinked unsaturated tails cannot pack tightly, so the membrane stays fluid enough to work in icy water. A common mistake is thinking saturated tails are the bent ones; saturated tails are straight.
column29: Think of butter versus oil in the refrigerator. Which one stays runny?

column9: A student wants to know whether apple juice or orange juice has more simple sugar. Which plan is the best test?
column14: Add the same amount of each juice and of Benedict's to two tubes, heat both in the same water bath for the same time, then compare colors
column15: Test apple juice with Benedict's and orange juice with iodine, then compare
column16: Use 2 mL of apple juice and 5 mL of orange juice, so the weaker juice has a fair chance
column17: Heat only the apple juice tube, since it is the one most likely to have sugar
column28: A fair test changes only one thing (the type of juice) and keeps everything else the same: the amount of juice, the amount of reagent, and the heating time. A common mistake is using different tests or different amounts, which makes the colors impossible to compare.
column29: In a fair test, what should be the only difference between the two tubes?

column9: Starch and DNA are both long polymers. Why can DNA store genetic information while starch cannot?
column15: DNA uses four different nucleotides whose order can vary, while starch repeats the same glucose unit over and over
column16: DNA is a lipid, and only lipids can store information
column17: Starch molecules are too small to hold information
column28: Information needs variety, like letters in a word. DNA's four bases (A, T, C, G) can be arranged in any order, spelling out instructions. Starch is the same glucose unit repeated, like typing one letter over and over. A common mistake is thinking size matters; starch molecules can be huge.
column29: Could you write a message using only one letter?

column9: Which pieces of evidence would show a sample is a nucleic acid rather than a protein? Select all that apply.
column14: It contains phosphorus in every monomer
column15: Its monomers contain the bases A, T, C, and G
column17: It contains carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen
column19: Every one of its monomers contains a sugar
column28: Phosphorus in every monomer, the bases A, T, C, G, and a sugar in each monomer all point to nucleotides. Nitrogen and C, H, O are found in both proteins and nucleic acids, so they can't tell them apart, and turning Biuret purple shows protein. A common mistake is choosing nitrogen, which both groups share.
column29: Pick only the clues that are true for nucleic acids AND false for proteins.

column9: In a lab, students burn 1 g each of sugar, butter, and dried egg white under identical cans of water. The sugar warms the water 8 °C, the egg white 8 °C, and the butter 18 °C. Which conclusion do the data support?
column14: All three released the same energy, because they all contain carbon
column15: Sugar released the most energy, because carbohydrates are the body's quick fuel
column16: Butter, a lipid, released more than twice as much energy per gram as the carbohydrate or the protein
column17: Egg white released no energy, because proteins can't be used as fuel
column28: The butter warmed the water more than twice as much (18 °C vs. 8 °C), so lipids hold more than twice the energy per gram of carbohydrates or proteins. A common mistake is mixing up quick energy with the most energy: carbohydrates are faster to use, but lipids pack more energy into each gram.
column29: Compare the temperature changes. Which food warmed the water most?

column9: Starch and cellulose are both long chains of glucose, yet a cooked potato is soft and a celery string is tough. What best explains the difference?
column14: Starch is actually a lipid, so it is soft
column15: Cellulose contains nitrogen, which makes it hard
column16: The glucose units are linked in a different way, so cellulose forms straight chains that bundle into tough fibers
column17: A potato's starch chains have more glucose units than celery's cellulose chains
column28: The same monomer linked a different way makes a different polymer. In cellulose, the glucose links make straight chains that line up side by side into strong fibers; starch's links make coiled chains that store energy. A common mistake is thinking the difference must be in the ingredients, when it is really in how they are put together.
column29: Both use the same building block. What else could make them different?

column9: Put these in order from smallest to largest.
column28: Atoms build amino acids, amino acids link into a polypeptide chain, four folded chains make one hemoglobin molecule, and millions of hemoglobin molecules fill one red blood cell. A common mistake is putting the polypeptide after hemoglobin; hemoglobin is built from polypeptides.
column29: Ask: which item is a part of which?

column9: How can a person build human muscle protein by eating beans, which contain plant protein?
column14: The body turns the starch in beans directly into muscle fibers
column15: Beans contain human DNA that builds the muscle
column16: Bean protein is already exactly the same as human muscle protein
column17: The body breaks bean protein into amino acids and links them in a new order to build its own proteins
column28: All living things use the same set of 20 amino acids. Digestion breaks plant proteins into amino acids, and your cells link them in the order your own DNA calls for. A common mistake is thinking the protein you eat goes straight into your muscles unchanged.
column29: What does digestion do to a protein, and what does the body do with the pieces?

column9: A green, unripe banana turns blue-black with iodine. A very ripe, spotted banana barely changes color with iodine but turns strongly orange with Benedict's. What best explains this?
column14: A ripe banana makes extra starch, which blocks the iodine
column15: The ripe banana's proteins turned into fats
column16: Iodine stops working on fruit with brown spots
column17: As the banana ripens, its starch is broken down into simple sugars
column28: Iodine tracks starch and Benedict's tracks simple sugar. Starch went down and simple sugar went up, so ripening breaks starch into sugars, which is why ripe bananas taste sweeter. A common mistake is thinking the tests stopped working, when the results actually agree with each other.
column29: Compare what each test detects in the unripe and the ripe banana.

column9: A cereal box claims "High in protein!" A student crushes the cereal in water and tests it. Biuret stays blue, iodine turns blue-black, and Benedict's turns orange. What is the best conclusion?
column14: The results do not support the claim; the cereal showed starch and simple sugar but no detectable protein
column15: The results support the claim, because Benedict's turned orange
column16: The cereal is mostly lipid, since iodine turned blue-black
column17: The cereal has no carbohydrates, since Biuret stayed blue
column28: Biuret staying blue means no detectable protein, so the data do not support the claim. Iodine (blue-black) shows starch and Benedict's (orange) shows simple sugar, both carbohydrates. A common mistake is treating any color change as proof of the claim; each test detects only one kind of molecule.
column29: Which test checks for protein, and what did it show?

column9: Ceviche is made by soaking raw fish in lime juice. Without any heat, the fish turns white and firm, much like cooked fish. What is happening?
column14: Lime juice adds starch that makes the fish firm
column15: The fish's fat turns into protein
column16: The acid in lime juice changes the shape of the fish's proteins, much like heat does
column17: Lime juice dissolves the fish's DNA, which turns it white
column28: Both heat and strong acid can denature proteins, unfolding them so they change texture and color. The amino acids stay the same; only the shape changes. A common mistake is thinking only heat can change a protein's shape.
column29: What else besides heat can change a protein's shape?

column9: Which of these chemical formulas is most likely a carbohydrate?
column28: Carbohydrates have only C, H, and O, usually in a 1:2:1 ratio. C₅H₁₀O₅ (ribose) fits exactly. C₁₈H₃₆O₂ has lots of hydrogen but very little oxygen, like a fatty acid (lipid). C₃H₇NO₂ has nitrogen, like an amino acid, and C₁₀H₁₄N₅O₇P has N and P, like a nucleotide. A common mistake is choosing C₁₈H₃₆O₂ because it is also only C, H, and O.
column29: Look for C, H, and O only, with twice as many H as O and about as many C as O.

column9: A student adds Biuret reagent to a tube of egg white and to a tube of plain water. BOTH tubes turn purple. What is the most likely explanation?
column14: Biuret turns purple when starch is present, and both tubes have starch
column15: Egg white has no protein, so its tube should have stayed blue
column16: The water tube was probably contaminated, so the test should be repeated with clean glassware
column17: Water always contains protein, so this is normal
column28: Plain water is the negative control and should stay blue. If it turns purple, something got into it, like protein left in a dirty tube or dropper, so the test must be repeated. A common mistake is trusting a result even when the control fails.
column29: What should the water tube look like if everything went right?

column9: Which statements about the four macromolecules are correct? Select all that apply.
column14: Carbohydrates and lipids can both store energy
column16: A protein's function depends on its folded shape
column17: Saturated fats have double bonds between their carbon atoms
column18: Phospholipids form the main structure of cell membranes
column19: Starch and glycogen are both made by animals
column28: Carbohydrates (starch, glycogen) and lipids (fats) both store energy, proteins work because of their shape, and phospholipids build cell membranes. Proteins contain nitrogen too, saturated fats have only single bonds, and starch is made by plants. A common mistake is the saturated fat statement: the double bonds are in unsaturated fats.
column29: Look for one wrong word in each false statement.

column9: Which example best shows how nucleic acids and proteins work together in a cell?
column14: Hemoglobin protein stores the instructions for building DNA
column15: A gene in DNA holds the instructions for building hemoglobin, and the hemoglobin protein carries oxygen
column16: Lipids copy DNA so that proteins can store energy
column17: Starch stores the cell's DNA until it is needed
column28: Nucleic acids hold the instructions, and proteins carry out the work. DNA's gene for hemoglobin tells the cell how to build the protein, and the protein then does the job of carrying oxygen. A common mistake is reversing the roles, as if proteins stored the instructions.
column29: Which macromolecule is the instruction book, and which one does the work?

column9: An athlete eats lots of protein but almost no carbohydrates or fat. Her body can still get energy by breaking down protein. Why is this a poor long-term plan?
column14: Protein used as fuel isn't available to build and repair muscles, enzymes, and other body structures
column15: Proteins carry genetic information, so burning them damages DNA
column16: Proteins contain no energy at all
column28: Protein can supply energy, but its main jobs are building and repairing tissue and making enzymes and other working molecules. Burning it for fuel takes it away from those jobs. A common mistake is thinking proteins have no energy; they give about the same Calories per gram as carbohydrates.
column29: What are proteins mainly used for, if not fuel?

column9: A student says, "Glucose and starch can't be related, because glucose is tiny and starch is huge." Which response best evaluates this claim?
column14: The student is right, because glucose is a lipid and starch is a carbohydrate
column15: The student is wrong, because starch is a protein made from glucose
column16: The student is right; small and large molecules are never related
column17: The student is wrong: starch is a polymer made of many glucose units, and it can be broken back down into glucose for energy
column28: Starch is a polysaccharide built from many glucose monomers. Size difference is exactly what you expect between a monomer and its polymer. A common mistake is thinking big and small molecules must be unrelated, when polymers are built from small monomers.
column29: Think about the relationship between monomers and polymers.
